title: University of Cambridge Biosciences DTP PhD Programme 2027: Fully Funded PhD Scholarship for International Students
summary: The University of Cambridge Biosciences Doctoral Training Programme (DTP) PhD Programme 2027 is now accepting applications from prospective doctoral students interested in pursuing advanced research in biological sciences in the United Kingdom. Supported by the Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council (BBSRC) Doctoral Landscape Awards, this programme offers fully funded PhD studentships designed to support talented researchers through doctoral study, interdisciplinary training, professional development, and research experience. The programme is an opportunity for eligible graduates to undertake PhD research at the prestigious University of Cambridge while benefiting from comprehensive financial support. Successful applicants will receive funding to cover university tuition fees and a stipend to help with living expenses. The programme also incorporates research rotations, professional internships, and opportunities to work with academic or industrial research partners, depending on the type of studentship selected. Applications are open to both UK and international candidates, including applicants from European Union (EU) and non-EU countries. However, the number of places available to international students is limited, making it important for prospective applicants to prepare strong applications and submit all required documents before the deadline. The application deadline for the 2027 entry is Tuesday, 8 December 2026 . Overview of the University of Cambridge Biosciences DTP PhD Programme 2027 The Cambridge Biosciences DTP PhD Programme provides doctoral training for graduates who want to develop their research expertise in biological sciences. Through its structured training model, the programme combines specialised research with broader academic development and professional experience. The programme is supported by BBSRC Doctoral Landscape Awards and is expected to offer approximately 25 studentships for the 2027 intake. These studentships are intended to enable successful candidates to concentrate on their doctoral research without having to cover the full cost of university tuition independently. The programme offers two main studentship pathways: Targeted studentships and Industrial Collaborative Awards in Science and Engineering (iCASE) studentships. Both pathways lead to doctoral research opportunities, but they differ in how students select their projects, gain research experience, and participate in professional or industrial placements. Applicants can apply for one or both types of studentships through the same application. They may select up to two projects, choosing projects from the same research area or from different areas. Applicants can select two Targeted projects, two iCASE projects, or one project from each pathway. This flexibility allows candidates to identify research opportunities that best match their academic background, interests, technical skills, and long-term career goals. Key Details at a Glance Programme: Cambridge Biosciences DTP PhD Programme Institution: University of Cambridge, United Kingdom Entry year: 2027 Funding provider: BBSRC Doctoral Landscape Awards Funding status: Fully funded studentships Expected number of studentships: Approximately 25 Annual stipend: Currently £21,805 for the 2026–2027 academic year Tuition fees: Covered by the studentship Available pathways: Targeted studentships and iCASE studentships International applicants: Eligible, including EU and non-EU candidates International student allocation: Up to 30% of the cohort Application method: University of Cambridge Applicant Portal Application deadline: Tuesday, 8 December 2026 Interviews: Conducted online Benefits of the Cambridge Biosciences DTP PhD Programme One of the most attractive features of this programme is its comprehensive funding package. In addition to financial support, students benefit from the academic environment of the University of Cambridge and a training structure that extends beyond an individual research project. 1. Full Tuition Fee Coverage Successful candidates will receive funding to cover their University of Cambridge tuition fees. This significantly reduces the financial burden associated with undertaking a doctoral degree at a leading UK university. For international students, tuition fees can represent a substantial part of the overall cost of studying abroad. Having these fees covered allows students to focus more fully on their research, academic development, and professional goals. 2. Annual Living Stipend The studentship includes a stipend to help students meet their living expenses during their PhD studies. The currently stated stipend is £21,805 for the 2026–2027 academic year . This is the published figure for that academic year; applicants entering in 2027 should check the programme s official information for the applicable stipend rate. The stipend is intended to contribute toward expenses such as accommodation, food, local transportation, and other day-to-day living costs. Prospective students should remember that actual expenses depend on individual circumstances and accommodation choices. Applicants should review the funding terms and the cost of living in Cambridge when assessing their financial needs. 3. Financial Support for International Students The Cambridge Biosciences DTP explicitly welcomes international applicants from EU and non-EU countries. For international students recruited through the BBSRC DTP, the programme states that it will cover student visa costs and the immigration health surcharge. It will also provide funding for tuition fees and a stipend to support living costs. This provision is particularly valuable for candidates who need to relocate to the United Kingdom for doctoral study. However, international funding is limited to a proportion of the incoming cohort. The programme can offer studentships to international candidates representing up to 30% of the cohort. For an intake of approximately 25 students, the programme gives the example of up to seven international studentships. Consequently, international applicants should pay particular attention to the strength of their academic records, their suitability for their selected projects, and the quality of their written application responses. 4. Research Experience at the University of Cambridge Students will undertake doctoral research within the University of Cambridge s academic and research environment. The programme s project-based structure enables students to develop specialised knowledge, investigate research questions, and strengthen their understanding of the research process. Depending on their selected project, students may also benefit from working with supervisors and research teams across relevant laboratories, departments, institutes, and partner organisations. This experience can help graduates develop skills that are relevant to academic research, biotechnology, scientific innovation, and other research-intensive career paths. 5. Professional Development and Internship Opportunities The programme incorporates professional experience into its doctoral training. Targeted studentship participants undertake a three-month professional internship with an organisation of their choice as part of their PhD journey. Students following the iCASE pathway undertake an internship of at least three months with an industrial partner connected to their doctoral project. These experiences can help participants understand how research is applied outside a conventional academic setting, develop transferable professional skills, and build connections with people working in relevant industries or organisations. 6. Research Rotations and Broader Scientific Exposure Targeted studentships include two research rotations. One rotation takes place in the laboratory associated with the project for which the student applied, while the second takes place in another laboratory selected according to its relevance to the targeted research project. This structure exposes students to more than one research environment and can broaden their understanding of the methods, perspectives, and scientific questions relevant to their field. It also provides an opportunity to explore related research approaches and develop a wider perspective on the subject area. 7. Opportunities to Build Professional Networks The programme includes training and networking as part of its broader doctoral development structure. Through research activities, internships, interactions with supervisors, and engagement with academic or industrial partners, students can establish professional relationships that may support their future careers. Such networks can be useful when pursuing postdoctoral research, scientific collaborations, biotechnology opportunities, or other positions that require advanced research expertise. The Two Available Studentship Pathways Applicants can choose between Targeted studentships and iCASE studentships. Understanding the differences between these options is important when selecting projects and preparing the application. 1. Targeted Studentship A Targeted studentship allows applicants to select projects from an advertised list of available research opportunities. Candidates should review the available projects carefully and identify those that correspond to their academic background, research interests, and relevant skills. The pathway combines a defined research project with broader research exposure and professional development. Key features of Targeted studentships include: Selection of one or more projects from the advertised list. Two research rotations, including one in the laboratory associated with the selected project and another in a relevant laboratory. A three-month professional internship with an organisation of the student s choice. Access to the programme s training and networking opportunities. An opportunity to develop specialised research knowledge while gaining experience in other relevant research environments. This pathway may be particularly attractive to candidates who want a structured doctoral research experience that includes laboratory rotations and professional experience beyond their primary research project. Before applying, candidates should consult the official project advertisements to understand the research questions, project requirements, and supervisor expectations associated with their preferred choices. 2. iCASE Studentship An iCASE studentship provides an opportunity to pursue a PhD within a University of Cambridge department while undertaking an internship with an industrial partner connected to the doctoral project. Applicants select their preferred project from the available iCASE opportunities. The industrial internship forms part of the overall doctoral experience and lasts for a minimum of three months. The relationship between the research project and the industrial partner gives students an opportunity to connect academic research with industrial applications. Key features of iCASE studentships include: Selection of a project from the advertised iCASE opportunities. Doctoral research within a University of Cambridge department. A minimum three-month internship with an industrial partner associated with the project. Research training and opportunities to develop technical expertise. Exposure to industrial research environments and potential real-world applications of scientific research. Access to programme training and networking activities. This pathway may be particularly suitable for applicants interested in understanding how scientific research contributes to industrial development, innovation, and practical problem-solving. Candidates should examine the details of each advertised iCASE project, including the industrial partner, research objectives, and relevant technical requirements, before choosing their preferred project. How Many Projects Can Applicants Select? Applicants can select up to two projects in the same application. The programme allows candidates to combine project types according to their interests and preferences. The permitted combinations are: Two Targeted studentship projects. Two iCASE studentship projects. One Targeted project and one iCASE project. The two projects may be within the same research area or across different research areas. Applicants should avoid selecting projects solely because they appear attractive or prestigious. Instead, they should consider whether their academic qualifications, previous research experience, coursework, technical skills, and long-term interests make them suitable for each project. Each selected project requires a statement of interest. Candidates should therefore prepare a separate, project-specific explanation of their motivation and suitability for every project they choose. Eligibility Requirements for the 2027 PhD Programme Applicants must satisfy the academic eligibility requirements specified by the programme and the University of Cambridge. Academic Qualifications The programme states that applicants should have achieved a High II.i Honours Degree . Applicants whose degrees were awarded outside the United Kingdom should consult the University of Cambridge s international qualifications guidance to determine the equivalent qualification in their country. Candidates should not assume that every bachelor s degree automatically meets the required standard. The University must assess qualifications according to its own equivalency and admissions criteria. Applicants who are still completing their undergraduate degrees should consult the official programme guidance to determine whether they can apply before graduation and what evidence of their academic results they must provide. APPLY HERE Research Interests and Relevant Skills Applicants should select projects that align with their academic interests and demonstrate that they are prepared for doctoral-level research. The application process requires candidates to explain their interest in their chosen projects and identify relevant research projects, experience, skills, or coursework that have prepared them for the proposed research. Although the precise academic or technical requirements may differ between projects, candidates should read each project advertisement carefully to determine the relevant expectations. A strong application should make a clear connection between the applicant s previous academic experience and the research they intend to pursue. International Eligibility International candidates are welcome to apply, including applicants from EU and non-EU countries. However, the availability of international studentships is limited. The programme states that international candidates may receive up to 30% of the cohort s studentships. International applicants should therefore verify their qualification equivalency, prepare the required supporting documents, and ensure that their selected projects match their academic background. Required Application Documents and Information Applicants should prepare the information required by the University of Cambridge Applicant Portal and the programme s project-selection process. 1. Academic and Professional References Applicants must provide two academic and/or professional references . References help the admissions team evaluate a candidate s academic preparation, professional experience where relevant, research potential, and suitability for doctoral study. Candidates should identify appropriate referees in advance and provide accurate contact information through the application portal. The programme permits candidates to submit their application before their references have been received. However, all references must be submitted by the application deadline for the application to be complete. Applicants should therefore contact their referees early, explain the deadline, and allow enough time for the references to be prepared and submitted. 2. Project Reference Candidates must enter the correct project reference in the relevant application field. The programme provides examples of project-reference formats, including TRG-YYY-XX and ICS-XXX-YY . Applicants must use the reference associated with their actual selected project rather than copying an example from the general application instructions. The recommended approach is to copy the reference directly from the official project advertisement and paste it into the application form. This reduces the risk of typographical errors or mismatches between the selected project and the submitted application. 3. Project Title Applicants must enter the project title exactly as it appears in the relevant advertisement. The project title must correspond to the project reference entered in the previous field. Before submitting the application, candidates should check that both the reference and title match the same project. Incorrect project information could create confusion during the assessment process. 4. Statement of Interest A statement of interest is required for each selected project. The statement should explain why the applicant is interested in the specific research opportunity and how their previous experience has prepared them to pursue it. Candidates should address the following points: Interest in the research topic: Explain the scientific questions or research area that attract you to the project. Motivation for selecting the project: Demonstrate why the particular project fits your academic interests and future goals. Relevant discussions with the supervisor: Include useful information from any discussions you have had with the project supervisor, if applicable. Previous research experience: Describe relevant research projects, laboratory work, or other academic activities. Technical and analytical skills: Identify skills that are relevant to the proposed research. Relevant coursework: Explain how previous studies have prepared you for the subject area. The statement should be specific to the selected project. A general statement that could apply to almost any PhD opportunity is less useful than a focused explanation of the candidate s research interests, relevant preparation, and reasons for choosing that project. Contacting a supervisor before applying is permitted and may help candidates understand the project. However, it is not compulsory, and pre-application discussions do not form part of the formal applicant assessment or selection process. 5. Written Responses About Research Potential As part of the application, candidates will be asked to provide short written responses addressing several areas of their research readiness and motivation. These include: Motivation for pursuing a PhD. Innovative thinking and problem-solving. Ability to work independently. Knowledge of recent developments in the relevant research area. Understanding of the research process. Relevant technical skills. Applicants should prepare thoughtful, evidence-based responses rather than relying only on broad claims about their enthusiasm or ability. For example, when explaining problem-solving skills, candidates can describe a research project, laboratory challenge, or academic task in which they identified a problem, considered possible approaches, and evaluated the outcome. When discussing independent work, applicants can provide examples of managing a project, conducting research, learning a technical method, or completing a substantial academic assignment. Responses should be accurate and relevant to the research opportunity. 6. Contextual Admissions Information The University provides an opportunity for applicants to submit additional contextual information about their undergraduate studies. This information can help the University understand the circumstances in which applicants completed their studies and achieved their academic results. Submitting contextual information is optional. Candidates who choose not to provide it can still submit their applications through the standard process. Applicants who believe that additional context would help explain their academic background may wish to review the University s contextual admissions guidance before deciding whether to complete the form. Step-by-Step Guide to Applying The application process requires candidates to identify suitable projects, prepare the necessary supporting information, and submit a complete application through the University s official portal. Step 1: Review the Available Research Projects Begin by visiting the official Cambridge Biosciences DTP website and reviewing the available Targeted and iCASE projects. Read the project descriptions carefully, paying attention to research objectives, relevant skills, academic expectations, and the type of research environment involved. Shortlist projects that match your academic background and research interests. Step 2: Choose Up to Two Projects Select up to two projects from the advertised opportunities. You may choose two projects within one pathway or combine a Targeted project with an iCASE project. Before making your final choices, consider whether you can explain your interest in each project and demonstrate relevant preparation for the proposed research. Step 3: Check Your Academic Eligibility Review the High II.i Honours Degree requirement and consult the University s international qualifications guidance if your degree was awarded outside the UK. Make sure you understand the relevant academic requirements before completing the application. If you are uncertain about the equivalency of your qualification, consult the University s official admissions guidance rather than relying on informal comparisons. Step 4: Prepare Your Statements Draft a separate statement of interest for each selected project. Your statements should explain your motivation, relevant academic background, previous research experience, technical skills, and suitability for the specific research topic. Also prepare the short written responses about PhD motivation, innovation, problem-solving, independent work, current research developments, research methods, and technical skills. Allow enough time to review your answers for clarity, relevance, and accuracy. Step 5: Arrange Your References Identify two suitable academic and/or professional referees. Contact them well before the deadline and ensure they know how and when to submit their references. Although the application can be submitted before the references arrive, the references must be received by the final deadline. Step 6: Complete the Online Application Apply through the University of Cambridge Applicant Portal. The course is listed as BBSRC DTP PhD in Biological Sciences . Enter the correct project reference and title for each selected project, complete the required application fields, and provide the supporting information requested by the portal. Check that the project details and all submitted information are accurate. Step 7: Review and Submit Before the Deadline Before submitting, confirm that the application contains the required information and supporting documents. Check the project titles, project references, statements of interest, written responses, and referee details. Remember that an application is not complete simply because the main form has been submitted. All required supporting documents and references must also be submitted by the deadline. Applications that are not complete by the relevant deadline will be withdrawn. Applications are considered together as a gathered field after the closing date in December. This means candidates should expect their applications to be assessed after the deadline rather than assuming that submitting early will automatically lead to an earlier decision. Stage 1: Project-Level Review and Initial Interview Supervisors and the relevant departments or institutes review applications for their advertised projects. During this stage, they assess candidates suitability for the research opportunities and shortlist applicants for an initial interview. The review may consider academic preparation, the relevance of the candidate s background, the quality of the written application, research motivation, and the match between the applicant and the proposed project. Candidates should be prepared to explain their academic interests, relevant experience, and reasons for applying to their chosen research opportunities. Stage 2: Interview With the DTP Research Committee Candidates who successfully pass the initial stage will be invited to a second interview with the DTP Research Committee. This provides another opportunity for the selection team to assess the candidate s suitability for the doctoral training programme. Applicants should be prepared to discuss their motivation for pursuing a PhD, their understanding of research, their approach to problem-solving, their technical preparation, and their interest in the relevant research area. Online Interviews All interviews will be conducted online. Applicants should ensure they have access to a reliable internet connection and a suitable environment for participating in an online interview. They should also review their selected projects and prepare to explain their research interests clearly. Candidates should consult the official application timeline for further information about interview dates and subsequent stages of the process. Important Information for International Applicants The Cambridge Biosciences DTP is open to international applicants, including students from countries outside the European Union. However, international candidates should understand how the funding allocation works before applying. Limited International Studentships The programme can allocate up to 30% of the incoming cohort s studentships to international candidates. For a cohort of approximately 25 students, the programme gives the example of up to seven international studentships. This is a maximum allocation rather than a guarantee that seven international candidates will be selected. The actual number of awards will depend on the programme s selection process and available places. Visa and Health Surcharge Support The programme states that it will cover student visa costs and the immigration health surcharge for international BBSRC DTP students who are recruited. It will also provide funding to cover tuition fees and a stipend to support living costs. International candidates should nevertheless read the official funding conditions carefully and verify the arrangements that apply to their individual circumstances. International Qualification Equivalency Applicants whose degrees were awarded outside the United Kingdom should consult the University of Cambridge s official international qualifications guidance. The High II.i Honours Degree requirement must be interpreted according to the University s standards for the applicant s country and qualification. Candidates should not assume that the name or duration of a degree alone establishes equivalency. Preparing a Competitive International Application International applicants should focus on demonstrating their suitability for their chosen projects. A strong application should clearly connect the candidate s academic background, relevant research experience, technical skills, and motivation to the proposed research. Applicants should also ensure that their statements are project-specific, their references are arranged in advance, and their supporting documents are submitted on time. Because international studentships are limited, careful preparation is especially important. Can Applicants Contact Supervisors Before Applying? Yes. Prospective applicants are welcome to contact supervisors directly to discuss a project and learn more about the research opportunity. Such conversations may help candidates understand the project s aims, the type of research involved, and the background or skills that may be useful. However, contacting a supervisor is not a compulsory part of the application process. The programme also states that pre-application discussions will not form part of the applicant assessment or selection process. Candidates who decide to contact a supervisor should keep their messages professional and focused. They can briefly introduce their academic background, explain their interest in the advertised project, and ask a relevant question about the research. Applicants should not delay their application while waiting for a supervisor s response, particularly as the application deadline is fixed. Application Deadline for the 2027 Intake The official application deadline is Tuesday, 8 December 2026 . Applicants must submit their applications and ensure that all required supporting documents and references are received by the relevant deadline. Although the University permits applications to be submitted before references have been received, outstanding references must still arrive before the deadline. Incomplete applications will be withdrawn. Candidates are strongly encouraged to begin preparing well in advance, particularly if they need to contact referees, assess international qualification equivalency, or prepare statements for two separate projects. Submitting early also provides additional time to check for missing information or errors in project references and titles. Official Application Link and Further Information Applicants should use the official University of Cambridge website to review the programme, explore available projects, check eligibility requirements, and access the application portal. Official programme website: Cambridge Biosciences DTP PhD Programme The University of Cambridge Applicant Portal should be used to submit the application. The course is listed as BBSRC DTP PhD in Biological Sciences . For enquiries about the programme, prospective applicants can contact: Email: bbsrcdtp@admin.cam.ac.uk Address: 17 Mill Lane, Cambridge, CB2 1RX, United Kingdom Applicants should consult the official programme website for the latest project advertisements, application timeline, funding details, and any updates relevant to the 2027 intake. Conclusion The University of Cambridge Biosciences DTP PhD Programme 2027 offers an opportunity for eligible graduates to pursue fully funded doctoral research in biological sciences at one of the UK s leading universities. With tuition fees covered, a stipend currently listed at £21,805 for the 2026–2027 academic year, research training, and structured professional experience, the programme provides a comprehensive foundation for advanced scientific development. Applicants can choose between Targeted and iCASE studentships, each offering a different combination of research experience, rotations, and professional or industrial internships. The programme also welcomes international candidates, including applicants from EU and non-EU countries, and provides specified visa and health surcharge support for recruited international BBSRC DTP students. However, the number of studentships is limited, and international candidates are subject to a capped allocation. Prospective applicants should therefore review the available projects carefully, confirm their academic eligibility, prepare strong project-specific statements, arrange two references, and complete every required application step. The most important date to remember is Tuesday, 8 December 2026 . Interested candidates should begin preparing early and consult the official Cambridge Biosciences DTP website for the latest information before submitting their applications. title: Aspen Healthy Communities Fellowship 2027: Leadership Training, Covered Programme Costs and a Stronger Voice for Community Change
summary: The Aspen Healthy Communities Fellowship 2027 offers a structured opportunity to strengthen the leadership, communication and advocacy behind community health initiatives. Delivered by the Aspen Global Innovators Group, the programme helps turn practical experience into a clearer public voice, stronger professional connections and more effective community action. The programme builds on a growing record: Aspen s April 2026 announcement described a network of more than 50 Healthy Communities leaders working across 17 communities. Its approach connects local expertise with a broader platform for exchanging ideas and advancing solutions. [2] About the Aspen Global Innovators Group The Aspen Global Innovators Group champions leadership grounded in the experiences of communities themselves. Its work brings together leadership development, strategic partnerships and advocacy tools to advance health and development. Its definition of innovation extends beyond a new product or technology. It includes responding to unmet needs, strengthening overlooked approaches and creating connections that help promising ideas produce lasting social benefits. This perspective matters because community health initiatives often depend on trust, local knowledge and cooperation. A useful solution must work within the circumstances of the people it is intended to serve. AGI s approach emphasizes strengthening the voices and influence of leaders close to those circumstances. [3] What the Healthy Communities Programme Develops Aspen s five-year impact report describes a year-long model combining tailored communication, narrative and leadership development with coaching. The training brings together several practical skills: Opinion writing: presenting a community issue and a clear argument for action. Advocacy planning: organizing ideas around a specific change. Media interviews: explaining expertise to a wider audience. Digital communication: making professional knowledge and community work more visible. Leadership development: reflecting on experience and strengthening the ability to guide change. [4] These skills can complement operational work. Delivering services and explaining why those services matter are different tasks; both deserve attention. A persuasive public message should connect the problem, the proposed response and the evidence of progress without losing the human experience behind the issue. Why Communication and Leadership Training Matter Aspen s 2023 programme announcement explained how media training, clearer messaging, narrative development and networking can expand the visibility of community-led work. It also described a regional approach that brings together leaders responding to related challenges through different methods. The value of this model is the combination of individual development and exchange. A leader can improve the way they present their work while also examining how others approach difficult problems. Historical programme activities have included curated media and communications training and executive coaching. These are examples of the programme s established approach rather than a published session-by-session timetable for 2027. [5] For someone managing a demanding initiative, dedicated reflection can be useful. It creates room to ask whether the work s purpose is clear, whether its results are being explained convincingly, and whether the right audiences are hearing its message. Programme Costs and Payment Aspen covers fellowship costs; participants are unpaid. [1] Cost coverage should therefore be understood as support for participation. It should not be presented as a salary, a cash award or guaranteed funding for the participant s organization. Before committing, prospective participants should consider both the scheduled activities and the practical arrangements needed to step away from their usual responsibilities. Questions about booking arrangements or reimbursement procedures can be raised directly with the programme team. Important Dates for the 2027 Intake Stage Date Nominations open September 30, 2026 Nomination deadline October 30, 2026 Status notifications Early December 2026 Programme begins January 2027 No closing time or timezone is published. [1] Preparing a submission ahead of the deadline leaves time to check contact details, revise the impact statement and resolve questions with the organizer. Participation and Time Commitment Four compulsory in-person meetings take approximately 3–4 days each . Other activities typically require around 5–10 hours monthly . [1] A practical preparation step is to discuss availability with colleagues or collaborators. Consider who would cover urgent responsibilities during travel and how regular writing or reflection time could fit into an existing workload. The programme should be approached as an active learning commitment. Its value will depend partly on the attention participants can give to developing their ideas and applying what they learn. The Programme in Practice: Learning from the Rio Grande Valley A November 2025 account from Methodist Healthcare Ministries offers a useful picture of how the programme has operated. During a final convening in Brownsville, participants explored local conditions, met community organizations and joined discussions about community-led change. Visits to border-area neighborhoods brought attention to interconnected barriers involving infrastructure, transportation, digital access and healthcare. Narrative training then helped participants connect professional work with their personal experiences and the experiences of the communities they served. The account highlighted Jorge Rodriguez and Monica Hernandez Sanchez, who described growth through storytelling, peer exchange and a deeper understanding of their own leadership. [6] This historical example illustrates an important learning principle: place, people and practical experience can inform leadership development together. It does not establish Brownsville as a confirmed location for the 2027 meetings. A Record of Training, Mentorship and Community Impact The five-year impact report records: 650 person-hours of training , delivered through more than 50 sessions. 450 person-hours of mentorship . 30 publications by participants. More than US$6 million raised to expand and deepen their work. [4] These are historical, collective achievements. They are not benefits automatically awarded to each new participant, and the fundraising total is not a funding package for the 2027 intake. The figures help show the kinds of activity the programme has supported: developing ideas, building professional confidence, communicating expertise and strengthening the work participants already undertake. Examples from the Previous Cohort Aspen s 2026 announcement introduced eight participants: Moises Arjona Jr. Sandra de la Cruz-Yarrison. Marcella Juarez. Ray Sanchez. Cassia Herron. Attica Scott. Christopher 2X. Lauren Muir. Their work covered diabetes prevention, maternal health, food security, healthcare access and mental health. The same announcement identified support from the Humana Foundation, Knapp Community Care Foundation, Methodist Healthcare Ministries, Legacy Foundation of Kentuckiana and Valley Baptist Foundation. These details describe the 2026 cohort and its partners , rather than confirmed 2027 places or funding arrangements. [2] How to Submit a Nomination Self-nominations are accepted. [1] Use the nomination form linked from the official programme page. The current form requests information about both the nominator and the candidate, including: Names and email addresses. Organization information. The candidate s city and state. Professional title and website. Relevant focus areas. An explanation of the nomination and the candidate s work in reducing community inequities. Its focus-area options include entrepreneurship, healthcare, food security and nutrition, housing security, criminal justice, maternal health, public health and an additional “Other” option. [7] The impact explanation deserves particular care. It is an opportunity to show what the person has done and why that work matters. Practical Guidance for Writing the Impact Statement The following suggestions are editorial preparation advice, not additional application requirements: Describe the issue precisely. Identify the problem and explain how it affects people s lives. Clarify the person s contribution. Separate the candidate s own responsibilities from the broader organization s activities. Use reliable evidence. Where available, include verified results, participation figures or examples of improvements. Explain the approach. Show how the work responds to community needs and what makes it effective. Connect experience with purpose. Explain how direct knowledge of the issue informs the candidate s decisions. Identify a development goal. Consider how stronger communication, advocacy or leadership could help the work progress. A strong account does not need inflated claims. A clear example of a problem addressed, a thoughtful explanation of the response and credible evidence of results will communicate more than broad statements about passion alone. Before submitting, check that the names, contact details, organization descriptions and website links are accurate. Keep a copy of the submitted text for reference. Continued Connection After the Programme Alumni opportunities include writing support, prize nominations, Aspen events and travel stipends. [1] Continued engagement can help participants maintain professional relationships and remain connected to a wider exchange of ideas. Specific opportunities should be understood as possibilities rather than automatic entitlements. Official Information and Contact For programme updates and access to the nomination form, visit the official Healthy Communities Fellowship page . Questions can be directed to HealthyCommunities@aspeninstitute.org . [1] Conclusion The Aspen Healthy Communities Fellowship 2027 brings attention to the leadership behind healthier communities. Its established approach combines communication development, reflection, coaching and professional exchange so that practical expertise can reach wider audiences. A thoughtful nomination should explain the work clearly, demonstrate its impact and identify how further development could strengthen it. title: MIT Solve Global Challenges 2027 Open with Over USD 1 Million in Prize Funding and Nine Months of Support
summary: MIT Solve is accepting applications for its 2027 Global Challenges , offering technology-based solutions a pathway to funding, expert support, and partnerships. The current round covers climate, economic prosperity, health, and learning, alongside the 2027 Indigenous Communities Fellowship . Selected Solver teams receive a US$10,000 grant , with additional sponsor prizes available under their respective conditions. The shared application deadline is 2 November 2026 at 12:00 p.m. Eastern Standard Time . The MIT Solve challenges directory also features partner initiatives with their own application processes. One currently open opportunity is Samsung Solve for Tomorrow , whose application phase ends on 23 November 2026 . This guide explains the current challenges, funding, programme support, application process, and selection timeline. Information was checked on 4 October 2026 . What Is MIT Solve and How Do Its Challenges Work? MIT Solve uses open innovation to identify solutions to difficult social and environmental problems. Its challenges connect innovators with resources that can help their work reach more people. The challenges page describes a research-based approach and reports: More than 110 challenges conducted. More than 30,000 solutions submitted. Submissions representing 190-plus countries . The platform brings together several routes. The Global Challenges lead to the Solver programme. The Indigenous Communities Fellowship addresses a dedicated community context. Custom challenges are developed with partners around specific problems and may offer different prizes or support. Consequently, an award announced for one initiative should not be assumed to apply to every listing. For readers exploring social innovation funding, the directory is useful both for finding current applications and understanding the kinds of problems Solve and its partners support. The practical starting point is the individual challenge brief: it defines the problem your solution needs to address. Solve interprets technology broadly. Digital tools such as software, SMS, AI, robotics, and drones are among the approaches it considers, alongside traditional, ancestral, and natural technologies. The essential connection is the practical application of science and evidence-based knowledge to the problem being addressed. MIT Solve Challenges Currently Open for Applications Opportunity Main focus Application deadline 2027 Global Climate Challenge Climate adaptation and lower-carbon ways of living and producing food 2 November 2026, 12:00 p.m. EST 2027 Global Economic Prosperity Challenge Financial resilience, quality work, and affordable housing 2 November 2026, 12:00 p.m. EST 2027 Global Health Challenge Equitable access to good health and quality care 2 November 2026, 12:00 p.m. EST 2027 Global Learning Challenge Closing education gaps and improving learning outcomes 2 November 2026, 12:00 p.m. EST 2027 Indigenous Communities Fellowship Technology and traditional knowledge supporting community goals 2 November 2026, 12:00 p.m. EST Samsung Solve for Tomorrow School and community problem-solving through STEM 23 November 2026 The official listings identify these opportunities as accepting solutions. The 2027 challenges opened on 22 September 2026 ; their programme year is 2027 even though applications close in 2026. The 2027 Global Climate Challenge The climate challenge focuses on solutions that help people adapt to a warming world while reducing emissions. Its priorities include: Lower-carbon, resilient cities through construction, retrofitting, mobility, and circular materials. Protection against heat, flooding, drought, wildfire, and other hazards. More resilient, low-emission, or nature-positive agrifood systems and regional supply chains. Restoration and sustainable use of oceans and coastal systems. The brief emphasises practical delivery within existing infrastructure, budgets, and local capacity. Technology should strengthen communities’ ability to make decisions and respond to climate pressures. As an application-writing approach, explain the specific climate risk or source of emissions you address. Then describe how your intervention changes it, how you will measure that change, and what it costs to operate. A project promising reduced food waste, for example, should distinguish measured reductions from future projections. Explaining the evidence behind an expected benefit makes the proposal easier to assess. The 2027 Global Economic Prosperity Challenge This challenge connects three foundations of lasting prosperity: financial resilience, access to quality employment, and safe, affordable housing . The 2027 priorities include helping households and small businesses handle financial obligations and shocks; creating routes into quality work as technology changes labour markets; and improving access to affordable, climate-resilient homes. Solve’s wider economic prosperity work supports technology that expands access to financial services, jobs, capital, and essential infrastructure. Examples in its portfolio include digital addressing, market access for small-scale fishers, and tools connecting displaced language professionals with clients. These examples illustrate the variety of approaches rather than prescribing a particular business model. For a stronger proposal, define the economic outcome you intend to change. More registrations on a platform may indicate interest, but sustained income, lower borrowing costs, secure housing, or improved job quality can show whether users are better off. Explain how your solution produces that outcome and what evidence you will collect to demonstrate progress. The 2027 Global Health Challenge The health challenge seeks technology that makes good health and quality care more equitable. Its priorities are: Maintaining care during outbreaks, climate emergencies, conflict, or financing disruptions. Improving prevention and management of noncommunicable diseases, mental health conditions, and care needs associated with ageing. Expanding primary care by supporting frontline workers and reducing barriers such as cost, distance, and administration. The brief also stresses community trust and the need to manage risks when using AI, including bias and privacy concerns. A useful proposal should describe the point in the care pathway where your solution helps. Explain who uses it, how it fits existing services, and what evidence supports its performance. Distinguish a tool that has been tested in practice from one whose expected benefits still need validation. This helps reviewers understand both the opportunity and the work required before wider implementation. The 2027 Global Learning Challenge The learning challenge looks for solutions that improve what learners actually understand and can do. Priorities include: Evidence-based support for teachers. Education in emergency or resource-constrained settings. Assistive and multilingual technologies. Better assessment and early identification of learning difficulties. The brief favours technology that deepens learning, preserves human relationships, integrates with curricula, and strengthens public education systems. For tools serving children, it highlights privacy, safety, fairness, human oversight, and responsible data governance. In preparing an education proposal, explain how learning gains will be measured. Usage statistics alone do not show whether reading, numeracy, practical skills, or other intended outcomes have improved. If your tool depends on connectivity or particular devices, explain how it will work in the settings you aim to serve. A convincing implementation plan should account for the conditions in which learning actually takes place. The 2027 Indigenous Communities Fellowship The fellowship supports solutions that combine technology with culturally grounded knowledge and community priorities. Its 2027 themes include energy and environmental sovereignty, stewardship and climate adaptation, ethical data and AI tools, economic opportunities, culturally grounded education and language revitalisation, and holistic health. Solve’s Indigenous Communities work places culture and traditional knowledge at the centre of solutions developed for and with communities. Its portfolio spans areas such as agriculture, energy, mapping, and financial services. A practical way to frame a proposal is to explain how community input has shaped the work, who guides important decisions, and how the benefits will endure. Solve also describes access to more than US$1 million in prize funding . Its FAQ reports average funding of around US$40,000 per selected team ; that average is not a guaranteed individual award. What the Nine-Month Solver Programme Provides Selected innovators receive unrestricted funding and join a nine-month support programme . The programme’s published resources include: Leadership coaching. Workshops on subjects such as business models, marketing, and impact measurement. Monitoring and evaluation support. Access to in-kind or pro bono resources. Connections with experts and other Solver teams. Opportunities for visibility and pitching. This combination can be particularly useful when a solution has demonstrated promise but needs help with implementation. For example, a team may need to refine its pricing, strengthen its evidence, identify a delivery partner, or prepare for expansion. Applicants should explain which of these barriers matters most to their project and how outside support could resolve it. The current challenge FAQ estimates approximately 25 hours of programme activities over nine months , with flagship events requiring additional attendance. Continued access to community resources and funding opportunities extends beyond the initial programme. The application guide states that late submissions are not accepted, including those affected by technical or connectivity problems. Programme participation and pitching are in English, and the designated team lead is expected to represent the solution during selection and programme activities. How to Apply to MIT Solve Choose the relevant challenge. Read its brief and focus on the problem your solution most directly addresses. Create an account or log in. Select the challenge and use the Start Solution option. Set up the submission. Apply through an individual account or a team; the platform supports invitations for collaborators. Complete the solution profile. Some challenges allow a reusable profile containing basic information about your work. Answer the application questions. Complete every required field and provide relevant optional information. Review and submit. A saved draft does not count as a submitted application. Refine before the deadline if needed. The platform permits edits to submitted applications before closing. The downloadable application questions are a preparation resource. Submission must take place through the online platform. Before you begin, it can help to assemble a short project description, evidence from testing, a realistic delivery budget, and an explanation of how the work will be sustained. These are preparation suggestions, not a substitute for the official application fields. How MIT Solve Evaluates Solutions The selection process includes screening, expert review, further judging, and finalist pitching. The published criteria cover: Challenge alignment. Potential impact. Practical feasibility. Innovation. Design informed by communities. Scalability. Partnership potential. Evidence that the technology works. Some criteria are considered from finalist selection onward. Use these criteria to check the logic of your submission. Can a reviewer follow the connection between the problem, the intervention, and the expected result? Have you separated existing evidence from assumptions? Does your expansion plan explain delivery capacity as well as demand? An application becomes easier to assess when it explains a few concrete points clearly: the people experiencing the problem, the change your solution enables, what has been tested, and the resources needed for the next stage. Avoid replacing those details with broad statements about innovation or impact. title: UCL Laws MPhil/PhD Scholarships 2027: Funding Opportunities, Eligibility and Application Deadline
summary: Are you planning to pursue an MPhil or PhD in Law and looking for funding to support your postgraduate research? UCL Laws offers several competitive scholarship and funding opportunities for prospective MPhil/PhD students. These funding opportunities are designed to support academically excellent researchers undertaking advanced legal research at University College London (UCL) . Available opportunities include Faculty of Laws Research Scholarships, Research Opportunity Scholarships, the BAME Research Opportunity Scholarship, the IBIL Intellectual Property PhD Scholarship, UCL Research Excellence Scholarships, and Global Centre for Democratic Constitutionalism PhD Studentships. For applicants hoping to secure funding, an important deadline is 19 November 2026 . Submitting an MPhil/PhD application by this date means applicants will be automatically considered for the funding opportunities listed by UCL Laws, although individual awards may have their own specific requirements. About the UCL Laws MPhil/PhD Programme The MPhil/PhD programme at UCL Laws is designed for students who want to undertake advanced, independent research in law. A research degree provides an opportunity to investigate a specific legal issue in depth, contribute to academic knowledge, and develop advanced research skills. Unlike a taught postgraduate programme, an MPhil/PhD involves substantial independent research under academic supervision. Students considering applying should therefore have a clear research interest and be prepared to undertake extensive academic investigation. UCL Laws MPhil/PhD Fees and Finance Before applying for an MPhil/PhD, prospective students should understand the financial commitments involved. Tuition fees cover the core elements of the programme, including: Tuition Registration Examination If additional research expenses apply, these may be specified in the student s formal offer of admission. UCL publishes tuition fees for each academic year through its official fee schedules. The fees for subsequent years may increase, meaning students should take potential annual increases into account when planning their finances. Tuition Fees for UK and International Students UCL provides separate information about postgraduate research tuition fees for UK and international students. The information currently available for the 2026–27 academic year provides an indication of what students may expect to pay, although fees for the following academic year may increase. Prospective students should therefore check the latest UCL fee information before making financial plans. Students should also consider whether their intended scholarship or funding opportunity covers tuition fees, living costs, or both. Living Costs for MPhil/PhD Students Tuition fees are only one part of the cost of undertaking postgraduate research at UCL. Students also need to budget for living expenses, particularly because UCL is located in London. Potential expenses include: Accommodation Food Local and international travel Study materials Personal expenses Other costs associated with living and studying in London Applicants should therefore develop a realistic financial plan before beginning their programme. Funding that covers tuition fees does not necessarily mean that all living expenses will automatically be covered, so applicants should carefully examine the terms of individual scholarships. UCL Laws PhD Funding and Scholarships UCL Laws provides several scholarship opportunities for prospective PhD students. The funding opportunities are competitive and are generally awarded on the basis of academic excellence . Importantly, applicants should first submit an application for a place on the PhD before applying for funding. UCL states that submitting a PhD application by 19 November 2026 will mean that applicants are automatically considered for the funding opportunities listed below. However, applicants should still read the information associated with each individual award because specific scholarship requirements may apply. 1. Faculty of Laws Research Scholarships The Faculty of Laws Research Scholarships are among the funding opportunities available to students undertaking postgraduate research in UCL Laws. These scholarships are intended to support strong candidates pursuing advanced legal research. Because the scholarships are competitive, applicants should demonstrate academic strength and present a well-developed research proposal. A strong application should clearly communicate: The proposed research topic The importance of the research The research questions being investigated The contribution the research could make The applicant s academic background The applicant s ability to undertake independent research Applicants should consult the latest UCL Laws scholarship information for the specific funding terms and eligibility requirements. 2. Faculty of Laws Research Opportunity Scholarship The Faculty of Laws Research Opportunity Scholarship is another funding opportunity available to prospective research students. The scholarship is intended to provide funding support for eligible applicants undertaking postgraduate research in law. Applicants should ensure that their academic and research background meets the requirements of the scholarship. As with other UCL Laws funding opportunities, academic excellence is an important consideration. 3. Faculty of Laws BAME Research Opportunity Scholarship The Faculty of Laws BAME Research Opportunity Scholarship is listed among the annual scholarship opportunities offered by UCL Laws. The scholarship is designed around widening participation and supporting eligible applicants from backgrounds represented within the award s eligibility criteria. Applicants interested in this scholarship should carefully review the current UCL requirements to confirm whether they qualify under the applicable criteria. 4. IBIL Intellectual Property PhD Scholarship The IBIL Intellectual Property PhD Scholarship is focused specifically on doctoral research relating to intellectual property . This opportunity may be particularly relevant to applicants whose proposed research falls within areas such as: Intellectual property law Innovation Copyright Patents Trademarks Technology and intellectual property Commercialisation of intellectual property Related legal and policy issues Applicants interested in pursuing doctoral research in intellectual property should review the specific requirements of the scholarship and ensure that their proposed research aligns with its focus. 5. UCL Research Excellence Scholarships The UCL Research Excellence Scholarships provide another potential funding route for high-achieving research students. These scholarships are designed to support academic excellence across UCL s research programmes. For an applicant to be competitive, academic achievements and the strength of the proposed research are likely to be important considerations. Students applying through UCL Laws should carefully review the relevant UCL Research Excellence Scholarship requirements in addition to the Faculty of Laws information. 6. Global Centre for Democratic Constitutionalism PhD Studentships The Global Centre for Democratic Constitutionalism PhD Studentships provide another potential source of funding for applicants whose research interests align with the centre s area of focus. The opportunity may be particularly relevant to researchers interested in topics connected to: Constitutional law Democracy Democratic institutions Constitutional development Governance Comparative constitutionalism Related legal and political questions Applicants should review the specific studentship information to determine whether their research proposal aligns with the centre s priorities. Important Application Deadline The key deadline stated by UCL Laws is: 19 November 2026 Applicants who submit their PhD application by this deadline will be automatically considered for the funding opportunities listed by UCL Laws . This makes the deadline particularly important for applicants who require financial support for their MPhil/PhD studies. Applicants should not wait until the final day if they can submit earlier. Preparing a strong research proposal, academic documents, references, and other required materials can take considerable time. Why You Should Apply Before the Deadline Submitting your application before the deadline is important because the funding opportunities are competitive. Applicants should allow enough time to: Develop a strong research proposal. Identify an appropriate research area. Review the MPhil/PhD admission requirements. Prepare academic documents. Check eligibility for individual scholarships. Complete the application correctly. Submit the application before 19 November 2026. Who Should Consider Applying? The UCL Laws MPhil/PhD funding opportunities may be suitable for applicants who: Want to pursue advanced research in law. Have strong academic backgrounds. Are interested in completing an MPhil or PhD. Have a clear legal research interest. Can develop a strong research proposal. Want to contribute to legal scholarship. Are interested in areas such as intellectual property, constitutionalism, democracy, or other areas of law. Require funding support for postgraduate research. Applicants should remember that individual scholarships may have additional eligibility criteria. How to Strengthen Your Application Because the scholarships are competitive, applicants should take time to prepare a strong application. Develop a Strong Research Proposal The research proposal is one of the most important parts of a research degree application. Your proposal should clearly explain: What you intend to research The central research question Why the topic is important The existing research or legal debate The gap your research intends to address Your proposed methodology The potential contribution of your research A clear and focused proposal can help demonstrate that you understand your research area and are prepared for doctoral-level study. Demonstrate Academic Excellence The scholarships are awarded competitively based on academic excellence. Applicants should therefore clearly present their academic achievements and relevant research experience. Where applicable, applicants can highlight: Previous degrees Academic results Research projects Publications Academic awards Conference participation Relevant professional experience Choose Your Research Area Carefully Applicants should ensure that their proposed research fits within the expertise and research interests of UCL Laws. This is particularly important for applicants interested in specialised scholarships such as the IBIL Intellectual Property PhD Scholarship or the Global Centre for Democratic Constitutionalism PhD Studentships . Understand the Financial Requirements Even when applying for scholarships, students should understand the full financial requirements of studying in London. Consider: Tuition fees Accommodation Food Transportation Research expenses Study materials Other personal living costs Applicants should carefully examine what each scholarship covers before assuming that all expenses will be funded. APPLY HERE Application Process The process begins with an application for a place on the MPhil/PhD programme. UCL Laws states that the PhD application should precede the funding application. Applicants should therefore focus first on meeting the academic admission requirements and submitting a strong research degree application. Submitting the PhD application by 19 November 2026 will result in automatic consideration for the listed funding opportunities. Applicants should nevertheless review the details of each award to understand whether additional steps or requirements apply. Additional Funding Options UCL also provides guidance on other potential sources of funding for postgraduate research students. Applicants who are not successful in one scholarship competition may therefore wish to investigate other funding opportunities available through UCL or external organisations. Exploring multiple funding options can be particularly important for international students because postgraduate study in London can involve significant tuition and living expenses. What International Applicants Should Know International applicants should carefully review UCL s requirements for postgraduate research students. They should consider: International tuition fees Visa requirements Living costs in London Available scholarships Funding coverage Research expenses Financial requirements for studying in the UK The scholarship information provided does not state that these opportunities are exclusively for UK applicants. However, eligibility varies between individual awards, so international applicants should check the specific requirements of each scholarship. Visit HERE to learn more about the UCL Laws MPhil/PhD Scholarships 2027 Countries and Regions The information provided does not establish one universal nationality requirement for all the UCL Laws scholarships. Eligibility can vary depending on the specific scholarship. Prospective applicants from outside the UK should therefore check the individual award requirements and UCL s requirements for international postgraduate research students. Applicants should not assume that every scholarship listed has identical eligibility criteria. Category of People Who Qualify The opportunities are primarily aimed at prospective MPhil/PhD students in Law who demonstrate strong academic ability and have an appropriate research interest. Depending on the specific scholarship, eligible applicants may include: UK students International students Applicants with strong academic backgrounds Prospective postgraduate researchers Applicants interested in intellectual property law Applicants whose research relates to democratic constitutionalism Applicants who meet the specific criteria of the relevant Faculty of Laws scholarship The Faculty of Laws BAME Research Opportunity Scholarship has specific eligibility criteria relating to the target group named in the award, while other scholarships may have different requirements. Applicants should check the individual scholarship conditions before applying. Key Information at a Glance Institution: University College London (UCL), Faculty of Laws Programme: MPhil/PhD in Law Funding: Multiple scholarship and studentship opportunities Basis of awards: Academic excellence and competitive selection Key application deadline: 19 November 2026 Automatic funding consideration: Yes, for the listed funding opportunities when the PhD application is submitted by the deadline Study location: London, United Kingdom Suitable for: Prospective MPhil/PhD researchers in Law Funding areas include: General legal research, research opportunities, intellectual property, research excellence, democratic constitutionalism, and related areas Conclusion The UCL Laws MPhil/PhD scholarships and funding opportunities provide prospective legal researchers with several potential routes to financial support for advanced postgraduate research. The available opportunities include the Faculty of Laws Research Scholarships, Faculty of Laws Research Opportunity Scholarship, Faculty of Laws BAME Research Opportunity Scholarship, IBIL Intellectual Property PhD Scholarship, UCL Research Excellence Scholarships, and Global Centre for Democratic Constitutionalism PhD Studentships . All of these opportunities are competitive, and academic excellence is an important factor in the funding process. One of the most important dates for prospective applicants is 19 November 2026 . Submitting an MPhil/PhD application by this deadline means that applicants will automatically be considered for the funding opportunities listed by UCL Laws, subject to the specific requirements of each award. Applicants should begin preparing well in advance by developing a strong research proposal, reviewing admission requirements, gathering supporting documents, and investigating the individual scholarship criteria. For students who are academically strong and interested in undertaking advanced legal research at one of the UK s leading universities, the UCL Laws MPhil/PhD funding opportunities could provide an important pathway toward postgraduate research. title: IMF Economist Program 2027: Apply and Launch Your Global Economics Career with the International Monetary Fund
summary: Are you a recent PhD graduate in economics or a related field looking to build a career as an international economist? The International Monetary Fund (IMF) Economist Program (EP) offers talented economists the opportunity to work on real-world economic policy challenges and contribute to issues affecting the IMF s 191 member countries . IMF Economist Program The International Monetary Fund s Economist Program (EP) is the IMF s flagship entry program for PhD economists . Designed for recent PhD graduates and economists completing their doctoral studies, the EP provides an accelerated introduction to the IMF s policy, analytical, and operational work. Through structured rotational assignments and direct engagement with economic policy issues, the program serves as a foundation for a long-term career as an IMF economist. The EP is not a trainee program. Participants join the IMF as economists and contribute from the outset to country work, research, policy development, and capacity development activities. The three-year rotational program gives economists hands-on experience across the IMF s work, from country missions and surveillance to policy analysis and research . About the International Monetary Fund The IMF is a global institution with 191 member countries . Its mission is to promote international monetary cooperation, financial stability, sustainable economic growth, and poverty reduction. Economists at the IMF work across a wide range of policy areas including: Macroeconomic surveillance Fiscal policy Monetary and exchange rate policy Financial sector analysis External sector assessment Debt sustainability Capacity development Policy research Working at the IMF provides a unique opportunity to apply economic expertise in a multinational environment, engaging directly with member country authorities, central banks, ministries of finance, international institutions, and policymakers around the world. IMF Economist Program Structure The Economist Program is a three-year rotational program based at IMF Headquarters in Washington, D.C. Participants complete two departmental assignments designed to provide broad exposure to the IMF s work and develop a strong foundation in macroeconomic policy and surveillance. Program Detail Information Duration 3 years Structure Two departmental assignments Location Washington, D.C. Eligibility Recent PhD or within one year of completion Application opens September Application closes December Start September of the following year Cohort size Approximately 20–30 per year Career path Long-term IMF economist career Program type Rotational economist entry program What Do IMF Economist Program Participants Do? During the program, participants rotate through two departmental assignments, joining economic teams working in regional and country-specific surveillance as well as on fiscal, monetary, balance of payments, debt, and related issues. Country Work and IMF Missions EP economists contribute to IMF Article IV consultations and country programs , analyzing economic developments and helping advise member countries. Country assignments may involve evaluating economic developments, assessing risks and vulnerabilities, contributing to policy recommendations, and participating in country teams. Policy Analysis Participants contribute to IMF policy advice on fiscal, monetary, financial, debt, and external sector issues , supporting IMF advice to member countries. Research EP economists contribute to research and analytical work that can inform IMF policy frameworks, analytical methods, flagship publications, and policy decisions . Research assignments often involve applying advanced economic methods to practical policy questions. Capacity Development and Teaching Participants may support training, technical assistance, and knowledge-sharing activities that help member countries strengthen institutions and policymaking capacity. IMF Economist Program Selection Process Throughout the selection process, the IMF assesses candidates analytical skills, judgment, communication abilities, and ability to apply economic thinking to real-world challenges . title: Solon Fellowship Program 2026: Fully Remote and International Fellowship Opportunity in Climate Policy, Environmental Leadership and Public Affairs
summary: The Solon Fellowship Program , organized by Elected Officials to Protect America (EOPA) , is offering an opportunity for motivated young professionals to gain practical experience in climate policy, environmental protection, public leadership, communications, research, fundraising, project management, and civic engagement. The fellowship is designed for individuals who want to contribute to projects with national and international policy relevance while working alongside current and former elected officials, environmental advocates, veterans, frontline leaders, and other professionals committed to protecting the environment and strengthening democratic institutions. Applications are currently being accepted for the Summer Cohort ’26 . The program provides fellows with an opportunity to participate in meaningful organizational projects, receive specialized professional training, develop relationships with elected officials and policy leaders, and potentially advance into more senior fellowship positions. Importantly, the fellowship can be completed remotely , from EOPA s offices in Rockland, Maine or Washington, DC , or internationally, making it potentially attractive to qualified applicants outside the United States. About Elected Officials to Protect America Elected Officials to Protect America (EOPA) is described as a nonpartisan network of current and former elected officials focused on protecting land, water, democracy, and environmental justice. The organization works at the intersection of: Climate policy Environmental protection Public leadership Democratic governance Environmental justice Energy security Climate finance Clean transportation Land and water conservation Public communication Policy advocacy EOPA s approach combines policy mobilization, education and training, and media and storytelling. According to the fellowship information, the organization has organized hundreds of elected officials across all 50 U.S. states and has also worked internationally. Its activities include supporting policy initiatives, educating lawmakers and civic leaders, producing media campaigns and documentaries, and creating opportunities for elected officials and emerging professionals to develop leadership and policy skills. What Makes the Solon Fellowship Different? The Solon Fellowship is not simply structured as a conventional work-placement program. Instead, fellows are expected to become involved in a range of organizational activities and may have opportunities to contribute to projects involving research, policy, communications, partnerships, fundraising, media production, and project management. The fellowship therefore provides exposure to multiple areas of public-interest work. For individuals interested in environmental governance, climate policy, international development, public administration, political communication, nonprofit management, sustainability, urban governance, advocacy, or public leadership , the program can provide a multidisciplinary professional experience.
